    #12603. Breaking: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3701 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US.
    • The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US.
    • While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

    The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

    While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

    Recent findings suggest that TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese company and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

    Industry observers note that TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

    “TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link claims.

    TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

    Recent findings suggest that TP-Link has pledged to assemble all new routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

    Industry observers note that companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

    Some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

    Recent findings suggest that the Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any upcoming technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

    “The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie remarked in a joint statement.

    The Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

    The US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”.

    Recent findings suggest that for the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security company Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, new additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List right now includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

    A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

    It has been revealed that “The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” said Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”.

    McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

    “The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a company, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”.

    Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre stated the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

    Sources indicate that mcIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any firm receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she said.

    TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft said in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

    Security expert Bruce Schneier stated there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

    Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier mentioned.

    With routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.”.

    Sources indicate that when asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese organization, Schneier said that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”.

    Industry observers note that TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier noted that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”.

    TP-Link says the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article mentioned, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”.

    Industry observers note that TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the tech giant doesn’t have any upcoming updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

    In a recent development, TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

    Several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

    The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, remarked in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

    “TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he stated. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese company. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”.

    TP-Link said in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”.

    In 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

    TP-Link’s response to Joyce said it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The company notes in a fact sheet that when routers provided to owners by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”.

    Florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”.

    In a recent development, last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

    “Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

    TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the company’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

    TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

    “Any time a tech giant has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” remarked Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

    Recent findings suggest that marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a manufacturer has larger concerns pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he stated.

    In a recent development, although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a manufacturer official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he said.

    “There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he remarked. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”.

    Kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the company’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

    It has been revealed that kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”.

    Industry observers note that kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the organization’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he said. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”.

    Kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he remarked. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”.

    Kovsky pleaded with government officials in a letter to the FCC last month for a quick approval. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building fresh, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”.

    Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

    Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency plans if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”.

    Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not right now manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”.

    Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she noted others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with onshoring plans.

    “I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she remarked.

    The FCC remarked the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”.

    In a recent development, although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

    Industry observers note that after the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre said.

    Under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

    “We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC remarked in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”.

    It has been revealed that the FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

    “The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill states.

    Recent findings suggest that the CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement noted the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”.

    Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google on Thursday unveiled that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
    • The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time.
    • Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google on Thursday unveiled that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.

    The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week declared the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping consumers sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

    Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

    According to recent reports, computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

    As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

    Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

    The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024.

    Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

    Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.

    Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

    The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

    On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.

    The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.

    But Hatfield told the Newly introduced South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.

    The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.

    “The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield noted.

    “His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.

    “His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”.

    Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.

    Hatfield noted the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.

    “His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he mentioned.

    Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.

    The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.

    Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.

    Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.

    His decisions to go to Sushi Train for dinner with his friend and undergo a minor elective surgery in the aftermath of the alleged murders indicated Lamarre-Condon was calm and at points “completely relaxed”, Hatfield alleged.

    But within days, the accused must have been “feeling the world closing in”, the prosecutor said.

    “He wants credit for handing himself in to police … but even in his last hours he’s there going to Bunnings, buying paint and painting the inside of the van … still trying to cover up what happened,” Hatfield told the court.

    Lamarre-Condon eventually helped police locate the bodies, but only after being told about the state’s no body, no parole laws.

    It has been revealed that “The bodies were left … for a further four days after he’s arrested,” Hatfield remarked. “Evidence all the while being destroyed.

    “Imagine the grief [of the families] on those four days.”.

    The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.

    Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.

    “It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.

    Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.

    The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

    • The feature can list multiple items on e-commerce platforms for you, among other things.
    • Google's Gemini app for Mac now has the ability to do repetitive tasks on its own.

    The feature can list multiple items on e-commerce platforms for you, among other things.

    Google's Gemini app for Mac now has the ability to do repetitive tasks on its own. The feature has been available to PC users for a while, but now the Mac app can also access Gemini's "Computer Use" capability. That means it can now see what's on your screen via screenshots, as well as click, type, scroll and navigate programs and websites for you. You can use the capability to automate tasks that would usually take several steps across programs and devices, as long as you tell Gemini what to do in natural language.

    The AI app will work on your tasks in a background window and will just give you a live preview in your chat. It will not be taking control of your screen or your cursor, so you can use your Mac computer like you always do. Of course, Gemini will only be able to use the apps and programs you've given it access to, and it will ask for your approval for key actions.

    In Google's announcement, it gave several examples for how you can use the upcoming capability. You can use it to list items for sale on platforms like eBay in batches. If you're selling a whole bunch of clothes, for instance, you can ask Gemini to go through the photos you took of them stored in a local folder, research their pricing, log their details and then stage their listings. You can use it to rapidly fill out local PDFs, such as shipping declaration forms. You can also use it to speed up creative work, such as getting Gemini to automatically turn a pencil sketch into a 3D model.

    AI toys still not ready for primetime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a latest report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research.
    • The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a latest report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

    Recent findings suggest that the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research. While some AI products made important safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

    The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

    In a recent development, R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny was originally available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney. The toy was previously listed on Amazon but was removed after this story's publication. Walmart also removed a third-party listing for the toy after PIRG reached out to the retailer about the product.

    "The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross remarked, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

    Given the research findings, Cross remarked she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

    PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three upcoming AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

    In testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

    It has been revealed that "Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

    The GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

    While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she said it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

    Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

    Industry observers note that in a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help.

    Sources indicate that "These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross said. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

    The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

    Amazon and Walmart removed the panda from their platforms Friday, following publication of this story and PIRG's outreach to the retailers.

    Recent findings suggest that “Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," Amazon told PIRG in a statement. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops.".

    Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

    It has been revealed that foloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

    Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

    According to recent reports, the Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester remarked they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

    Despite this progress, Cross stated there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

    According to recent reports, even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross mentioned.

    Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

    Cross also stated some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

    ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

    The model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

    Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

    "We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross noted. "There's a lot of unanswered questions.".

    UPDATE: Nov. 20, 2026, 10:25 a.m. PST This story was updated to reflect Macy's and Amazon removing the GoLabs AI Panda from their platforms.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1184 w)

    Tech Report: Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) review: Minor upgrades that cost too much

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Meta's very best AI glasses are only slightly better than other recent models.
    • You'd be forgiven if you came out of Meta Connect feeling like Meta's third-generation Ray-Ban glasses seemed like a bit of an afterthought.
    • Industry observers note that compared with other recent glasses from the company, there's not that much latest to report.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Meta's very best AI glasses are only slightly better than other recent models.

    You'd be forgiven if you came out of Meta Connect feeling like Meta's third-generation Ray-Ban glasses seemed like a bit of an afterthought. The latest model was unveiled alongside the company's new audio-only glasses, its first VR glasses and an updated lineup of cheaper Meta-branded frames.

    Industry observers note that compared with other recent glasses from the company, there's not that much latest to report. Meta's latest Ray-Ban glasses have gotten some cosmetic updates and a few performance upgrades around the edges. There's still a lot to like; the frames are the most premium Meta-branded smart glasses without a display. But considering just how many variations of frames the company now makes, it's not clear that the $449 Gen 3 glasses should be your default choice if you're looking to invest in a new pair.

    Industry observers note that for now, the third-gen Meta Ray-Ban glasses only come in three frame styles: there's the classic Wayfarer frames, which have gotten a bit slimmer; Zena, a fresh cat-eye shape and Aviator, which Meta says is a tribute to the classic Ray-Ban design. As usual, each style is available in a number of different frame colors, many of which are semi-transparent so you can see some of the inner components if you look closely.

    Recent findings suggest that for this review, I wore a pair of Aviator frames in a brown tortoiseshell color called Havana. I've spent a lot of time in previous reviews complaining about glasses only coming in dark, boxy frames, so I was excited to see two new shapes. But it is disappointing that both the Zena and Aviator frames start at an eye watering $529.

    Maybe it's because the new, bolder frame shapes aren't for everyone. I've owned many aviator-style sunglasses over the years, but these felt the most oversized. They are 10mm wider than the smallest Gen 3 Wayfarer frames and it definitely showed on my face. I also felt a little silly wearing thick aviator glasses with clear lenses. I understand Meta offers clear transition lenses as the default choice for most of its AI glasses because it gives people more flexibility in how they wear them. But I think this particular frame shape is better suited to sunglasses.

    The bulkiness of the frames also caused some issues with the fit. The glasses constantly slipped down my nose to the point where I considered buying after-market silicon tips to keep them in place. The glasses' tips are technically adjustable, but unlike some other Meta Glasses that offer DIY adjustments, Ray-Ban Meta frames need to be adjusted professionally by an optician or at a Meta store. That's not a big deal if you buy a pair at one of these physical establishments, but it's kind of a pain if you order online.

    The other major noticeable change with Gen 3 is the addition of the action button, which has appeared on other recent models of Meta glasses. It's basically a customizable shortcut that lets you trigger a specific action without a voice command. I like to set mine to "read my latest text message," but you can use it for just about any Meta AI query.

    Under the hood, Gen 3 comes with two upgrades compared with Gen 2. It has a slightly better battery life, with the frames lasting "up to 9 hours" on a single charge and the charging case adding an additional 50 hours. That's about an hour better than Gen 2, but as usual, battery life can vary significantly depending on how you use them. I was able to squeeze about six hours of continuous audio playback on my pair. Features like Live AI, which uses the camera to analyze your surroundings, will drain the battery even more quickly.

    Gen 3 also comes with an extra microphone, which Meta claims should improve the sound quality for phone and video calls you take with your glasses. I never got any complaints with the five-mic setup on Gen 2, but people I spoke to on the phone while wearing Gen 3 assured me that I sounded clearer than I do on my AirPods Pro 2.

    Recent findings suggest that the latest glasses come with all the same Meta AI features as the rest of the company's lineup. The AI assistant is now powered by Muse Spark, which has generally made conversations feel more natural and reduced errors. I do miss the celebrity voices, though.

    Speaking of voices, Meta has made it clear that its smart glasses will be even more crucial to the manufacturer as its AI agent Muse advances. The company previewed Muse on its glasses during Connect, but the feature hasn't officially rolled out yet, though a Meta support page describes it as being in "beta." Once Muse is available on the device, you'll be able to chat with your agent via your glasses and "show" it what you're seeing through the glasses' cameras. That obviously opens up a lot of interesting possibilities, though it's hard to say how big of a deal this will actually be.

    In a recent development, I also worry that Muse and other AI features are likely to become a vehicle for Meta to more aggressively hawk Meta One subscription aims. The manufacturer has already shown a willingness to paywall some features, like its fresh hearing enhancement tool (which has yet to roll out). The company also seemingly considered a similar move with its other hearing-related feature Conversation Focus, which also has yet to fully roll out despite being announced more than a year ago.

    Recent findings suggest that one setting I am grateful to have is the ability to opt out of allowing the organization to train its AI models on "visual data" collected by your glasses. That means that when you ask Meta AI a question about something you're looking at, the glasses will not store that image and won't show it to contractors the company employs. That addition doesn't address all the privacy concerns people have about this product, but it's an improvement nonetheless.

    When Meta rolled out its Gen 2 Ray-Ban glasses last year, they were an obvious choice. But a lot has changed since then, and I'm not sure Gen 3 makes sense for most people. Meta's non-Ray-Ban glasses come with basically the same features for a starting price of $249. If you want the more premium finish that comes with the Ray-Ban branding, Gen 2 is still a solid option for $349, and you can still buy Gen 1 frames for $224.

    In a recent development, so while Gen 3 can still be fairly considered "top of the line" for non-display enabled glasses, it's a much more minor distinction at this point. With all the options now available, I think the only reason to choose Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 is because you love the Ray-Ban styles (no shame in that!) or you really want that extra bit of battery life. I suspect for most people, that's not quite enough.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that it’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica.
    • So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that it’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

    So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

    Sources indicate that but I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

    Since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re key. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

    Industry observers note that I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an key backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

    Industry observers note that focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s newly introduced in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the substantial questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

    But I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

    Recent findings suggest that one reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

    The former is crucial because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

    Recent findings suggest that all of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

    According to recent reports, but it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

    Industry observers note that it’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

    According to recent reports, we’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

    In a recent development, I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Former opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he becomes eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March.
    • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • The New South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, indicates she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he becomes eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March.

    Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

    The New South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, indicates she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.

    In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman remarked he would not run again in his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

    A third of the 24 current Liberal MPs have revealed they will not recontest their seat in March, including Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.

    In a press conference on Friday, Sloane insisted the departures were not an indictment of the party’s election prospects.

    Sources indicate that “No, that’s not the truth. What we are seeing is an impressive cross section of abilities and talent and tenure in our party,” she told reporters in the same room where, exactly a year ago, Speakman announced he would resign as Liberal leader in her favour.

    “We have people who have been in government before. We have people who have been in for a medium amount of time, and we’re going to have people with fresh ideas.”.

    Sloane stated she had tried to convince Speakman to stay and said many of the MPs leaving had been in parliament for more than 10 years, although Lane is a first-term MP.

    Sloane noted a significant number of Liberals had retired before the 2023 election, in which the Coalition lost government and the party dropped nine seats.

    Industry observers note that asked if she could guarantee that further MPs would not step down ahead of the March vote, Sloane said: “Look, I certainly hope not. I certainly hope not. I’m pretty sure that’s done. I’m pretty sure that’s done.”.

    Since last year’s leadership spill, the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.

    Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is now at 26%.

    According to recent reports, last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.

    On Friday, Sloane rejected the claims from “anonymous names in a Financial Review article”, saying the Coalition only needed to flip six Labor seats to form minority government.

    In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, said the Liberals were “said to face an existential threat” following a wipeout at the 2025 federal election and an “orange wave that seems to be coming across the country”.

    He warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.

    Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman remarked Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.

    “You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.

    According to recent reports, “I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”.

    Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.

    He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

    On Thursday, he stated being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

    He noted his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

    Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, unveiled the former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

    On Friday, Sloane mentioned Raffoul had been talking to her about Liberal party roles “only two months ago”.

    “She’s decided to chase personal ambition. She’s a very ambitious person, but she’s changed sides, and that’s a decision Chris Minns has made.”.

    Earlier, the NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, rejected the idea that One Nation was pushing Labor to become “Liberal lite”, saying Raffoul’s candidacy reflected “a journey that I think many Liberal people are going through as well”.

    Tech Report: You can reveal the full GTA 6 map in minutes using this simple plane trick

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (460 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Clear up that fog in no time at all, but be careful.
    • Industry observers note that GTA 6 has a huge map, which is around twice as big as the one found with GTA 5.
    • In a recent development, fog is obscuring every part of the map that you haven't explored yet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clear up that fog in no time at all, but be careful.

    Industry observers note that GTA 6 has a huge map, which is around twice as big as the one found with GTA 5. That's a whole lot of Florida-inspired strip malls and alligator-soaked swamps. However, new players start the game in a fairly remote region, based on the Florida Keys, and the vast majority of the map is unavailable for perusal.

    In a recent development, fog is obscuring every part of the map that you haven't explored yet. New regions get uncovered as you travel through them. You could do this the long way, by following the story. You could also do this the slightly-shorter way, by grabbing a car and just driving north until the wheels fall off. GTA 6 doesn't have a system in place that automatically ups the wanted level as you enter new areas, so that's good.

    It has been revealed that however, the quickest way to unlock the full map is found in the skies, and not the roads. Long-time players know the drill. Jason needs to get an airplane.

    Recent findings suggest that luckily, there's a plane just a few miles north of Jason's first house in Key Lento. Take a break from making home renovations and head to Southpoint Airfield, as seen in the map above. It's basically just north of the starting area.

    Drive the western bridge that runs over the Shoeless Keys and then head west a little bit onto a runway. It's hard to miss. The area is marked as restricted, but it's mostly abandoned so there shouldn't be any armed onlookers.

    Once at the airfield, look for a duster plane just waiting to be flown. Hop in and do your thing. Planes move incredibly fast and will rapidly unlock all of those foggy areas. Just fly carefully and keep an eye on fuel.

    You probably won't be able to get the whole map done on a single fly through, due to that fuel, but planes automatically regenerate at airfields as soon as one leaves. Fly back to Southpoint and start again, this time heading in another direction. You'll have the whole map uncovered in minutes.

    It has been revealed that happy travels. The only real thing to worry about here is the Mile Zero Air Station at the bottom left of the map. Flying over that airspace will instantly generate a four-star wanted rating. This wanted level can bring police after you in helicopters, so airplanes aren't necessarily safe. Save this area for last and exit as soon as the fog lifts from the map. Mile Zero is home to some really fast aircraft, but it's likely not worth the trouble just yet.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees.

    As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy.

    In a recent development, first, the firm’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold.

    The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has remarked it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans.

    Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A firm spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF.

    Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company noted that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.

    Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.

    Sources indicate that all told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.

    Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact.

    Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can. And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees.

    #12583. Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives.
    • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • Four babies who died in Newly introduced South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives.

    Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

    Four babies who died in Newly introduced South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.

    Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.

    The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

    In a recent development, baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.

    His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.

    The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

    Expert neonatologist and associate professor Nicholas Evans said on Friday that Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.

    It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.

    Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks mentioned it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.

    Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.

    “The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”.

    Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

    Recent findings suggest that experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but Evans told the court that it was ultimately most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

    Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation had arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.

    “If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”.

    Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.

    The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.

    But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.

    Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid-August.

    That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the problem.

    “The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans stated on Friday.

    Expert midwives earlier told the court they didn’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks because it was so rare.

    A 19 August ultrasound revealed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.

    Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.

    The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.

    In a recent development, baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.

    Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.
    • This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.
    • In the latest lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

    This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

    In the latest lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

    The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”.

    Recent findings suggest that neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings says that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

    DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”.

    In a recent development, multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

    In a recent development, the Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

    But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

    As of 2026, DraftKings released “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

    It has been revealed that “Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

    According to recent reports, “Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”.

    In June 2026, DraftKings launched what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”.

    Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

    Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

    It has been revealed that “Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
