    Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report!
    • Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker.
    • Fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE mentioned it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation’s most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX revealed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we’ll see you again the first week of December.

    Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker. Finnish satellite developer ICEYE confirmed Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space firm, Ars reports. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.

    Fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE mentioned it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements. Most of ICEYE’s satellites have introduced on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. With Falcon 9’s retirement on the horizon, ICEYE’s satellites will need rides to orbit. Avio’s Vega C rocket has a healthy backlog of contracts for European governments, but it hasn’t been a hit commercially. Investment from ICEYE could shore up Avio’s Vega rocket program and perhaps accelerate development of a new rocket.

    It has been revealed that NATO unveils launch brokerage initiative. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite launch network and help neutralize risks to the space systems on which it relies, Bloomberg reports. NATO launched two initiatives on Tuesday: Starlift, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets, and the Global Data Marketplace, which will bolster the alliance’s military operations in space with commercial data and services.

    Swimming in launches … Starlift will allow participating countries—Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and South Korea—to pool their military launch requirements and secure launch slots on commercial rockets. The NATO initiative will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed in a crisis. Bloomberg reported NATO’s tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, AI, cyber, and command-and-control networks.

    Recent findings suggest that stoke wraps up booster engine development. Stoke Space has completed development of its Zenith engine, the methane-fueled powerplant that will propel the organization’s medium-class Nova rocket off the launch pad. Stoke made the announcement in a social media post Thursday. “As flight engines clear acceptance testing, we’re shipping them down to Cape Canaveral for integration with Nova’s first stage—every week,” Stoke said. Seven Zenith engines will power the Nova rocket’s reusable first stage booster, combining to generate about 700,000 pounds of thrust at full throttle.

    Industry observers note that all eyes on Stage 2 … Stoke declared it cleared a “proto-qualification” milestone on Stage 1 earlier this year. Stage 2 is undergoing cryogenic proof testing and a hot-fire test campaign at Stoke’s test complex in rural Washington. Nova’s second stage is the real innovation, with a unique arrangement of 24 thrusters surrounding a regeneratively cooled heat shield to protect it during reentry back into Earth’s atmosphere. With this, Stoke aims to fully reuse both Nova stages. The first launch is currently expected sometime next year.

    Soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East. A Soyuz-2.1b rocket made its first and only launch from Russia’s Vostochny Cosmodrome this year, RussianSpaceWeb.com reports. The rocket’s Fregat upper stage deployed a latest pair of high-resolution imaging satellites, along with a cluster of smaller payloads, following liftoff from Russia’s Vostochny launch base on November 14 (local time). Vostochny, located in Russia’s Far East, hosted its first space launch in 2016. By some measures, Russia spent more than $5 billion building Vostochny, only to use it for an average of two launches per year.

    In a recent development, what was onboard? … Soyuz and Fregat carried two dual-use imaging surveillance satellites. A pair of CubeSat-class satellites for a Russian arms manufacturer were also onboard. These satellites are owned by NPO Kaisant, which specializes in drone communications and counter-drone weapons. NPO Kaisant says the satellites will join a constellation providing secure communications to Russian drones over Ukraine. A total of 12 secondary payloads were reported to be onboard, according to Roscosmos.

    It has been revealed that china’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone. Three months after landing its first orbital-class rocket booster, Chinese rocket company LandSpace claims it has completed “ground acceptance and testing” of the nine methane-fueled engines recovered from the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket, according to Guandian News, a Chinese outlet focusing on the country’s financial and economic sector. The engines were disassembled, inspected, refurbished, reassembled, and retested after flying to space and back in August.

    But wait … LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to successfully land its booster after an orbital launch attempt. The manufacturer did not say whether any of the nine engines will fly again, but don’t count on the entire Zhuque-3 booster stage from the August flight making another trip to space. The Zhuque-3 first stage toppled over soon after a seemingly flawless touchdown at LandSpace’s downrange recovery zone in northwestern China. Based on this week’s news, it appears engineers were able to salvage the engines.

    SpaceX makes a historic catch. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, took a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket with the first successful catch of its enormous Starship upper stage on November 14, Ars reports. It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment. SpaceX’s ability to recover and quickly relaunch Starships and Super Heavy boosters is central to all of the manufacturer’s lofty commercial ambitions and many of America’s high-level strategic imperatives, from national security to maintaining dominance in space exploration.

    What was it like to be there? … Ars Space Editor Eric Berger covered the launch and catch of Starship from a nearby perch at Starbase, Texas. “Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower,” Berger writes. “It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks. Nevertheless, it happened.”.

    Vulcan fails to deliver for Amazon. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry, Ars reports. Aside from ULA itself, the fallout from the failure will strike the US military and Amazon hardest. Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is also on contract to launch roughly half of the US Space Force’s national security missions over the next few years.

    Identifying the cause … ULA mentioned Wednesday that the failure was caused by inadequate fuel supply to the first stage engines, Ars reports in a follow-up story. “ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the tech giant said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.” This is fantastic news for Blue Origin, which builds the BE-4 and uses a similar design on its own Latest Glenn rocket. Vulcan’s solid rocket boosters also performed as expected Sunday after experiencing nozzle failures on two prior Vulcan flights.

    Google taps Blue Origin for AI launch. Blue Origin confirmed Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that manufacturer’s Project Suncatcher program, Ars reports. Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

    Hitching a ride … Google snatched up a ride on New Glenn just as US commercial heavy-lift rockets are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has launched three times to date. The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a company to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

    It has been revealed that relativity makes progress with Terran R. Another latest rocket is moving closer to the launch pad. Relativity Space’s partially reusable Terran R rocket could launch sometime next year if engineers can finish development with no major setbacks. Relativity posted an patch on YouTube this week, detailing several recent achievements at several of the organization’s locations across the country. At Relativity headquarters in Southern California, teams have completed Terran R’s first stage thrust structure with a full set of 13 Aeon engines, fluid lines, and avionics. The engine compartment is now being integrated with Stage 1 tankage. Terran R’s second stage recently completed its first all-up test firing at Stennis Space Center, Mississippi.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, at Cape Canaveral … Relativity is also moving forward with the Terran R launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The launch pad’s lightning protection towers are now complete, as is the steel framing for Terran R’s launch table. Work continues on the rocket’s transporter-erector, strongback, and the launch pad’s propellant storage tanks.

    November 20: Long March 8A | SatNet LEO Group | Wenchang Space Launch Site, China | 11:59 UTC.

    November 21: Falcon 9 | USSF-317 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 02:32 UTC.

    November 21: Long March 6C | Unknown Payload | Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, China | 03:50 UTC.

    Sources indicate that first of all, the aesthetics are on point. It looks more like a record player than something that runs compact discs. The CD is exposed and spins atop the device for all to see. It features clips that allow it to connect with recent TE products like the EP-35 portable speaker and the K.O. II groove machines.

    It has been revealed that there's a line of red LEDs that light up to show volume across the left and right channels, which look pretty neat in action. There's also a box that indicates the precise timecode and other track-specific information.

    Recent findings suggest that the EP/BC-1 can do something else that traditional CD players typically can't: speed up or slow down tracks via a varispeed dial. This should be very useful to DJs who are looking to beatmatch when transitioning between songs. To that end, there's a built-in beat detection algorithm with the ability to output tempo in sync.

    Industry observers note that the unit can also rip audio CDs to digital files and streams via Bluetooth and Auracast. It's a portable device that charges via USB-C. Finally, there's a headphone jack for solo listening.

    It has been revealed that teenage Engineering is calling this the first entry in a upcoming lineup called the "Broadcast Series." We don't know what's coming next, but it sounds like this line will feature audio products that could be used to broadcast stuff. My bet would be a cassette player or maybe another mixer. The EP/BC-1 CD player is available for purchase right now. It costs $329.

    This leads me to the synth-sized elephant in the room. Teenage Engineering got famous making musical instruments but rumors persist that the company is phasing out that market segment entirely. TE has made some of my favorite (though expensive) instruments of all time, so a phase-out would be an absolute shame. TE has had mixed results when dabbling in other markets.     Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • CT scans before (left) and after treatment with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and nabpaclitaxel) showing multiple tumours that are no longer visible.
    • Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
    • Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CT scans before (left) and after treatment with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and nabpaclitaxel) showing multiple tumours that are no longer visible. Yellow arrows indicate the tumours visible before treatment.

    Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.

    Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.

    Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

    But doctors stress it is unclear how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.

    Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.

    The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this latest drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.

    "We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue.".

    Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.

    Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.

    Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.

    Doctors hope the upcoming treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.

    The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.

    Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.

    tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients.

    just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear.

    for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans.

    Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

    "We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he stated.

    Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, external, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

    Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

    Dr Godfrey noted: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers.".

    Recent findings suggest that he remarked longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed.".

    Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTCâNCIâAACR Symposium 2026, external where the work is being presented to other doctors, stated: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again.".

    Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year, external.

    In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

    Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

    Symptoms can include, external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Want to see your live AI usage on your Mac’s icons? This clever fresh app lets you

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that there’s a newly introduced way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons.
    • Recent findings suggest that designer Michael Flarup has just rolled out a fresh Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation.
    • Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that there’s a newly introduced way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really!

    Recent findings suggest that designer Michael Flarup has just rolled out a fresh Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage.

    Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app.

    Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!).

    Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget. But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.).

    Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools.

    There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own.

    Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio, and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers.

    He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data.

    Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time.

    Recent findings suggest that “The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said.

    That lets customers configure icons to do all kinds of fun, upcoming things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking.

    Recent findings suggest that “That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added.

    The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website claims.

    SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.
    • The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious looks to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space.
    • According to recent reports, spaceX has stated it aims to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.

    The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious looks to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

    According to recent reports, spaceX has stated it aims to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

    It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

    The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

    The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

    SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

    The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people noted. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

    The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

    More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

    Sources indicate that apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

    Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

    SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

    Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

    The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

    “The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

    “This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he mentioned.

    Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in Fresh York.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’.

    China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

    The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it remarked was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

    The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

    The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

    “We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”.

    Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

    It has been revealed that some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

    The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

    “The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” remarked Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

    Analysts had remarked that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

    In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

    First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and indicated that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”.

    The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

    Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”.

    According to recent reports, xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

    Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

    According to recent reports, european allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, mentioned in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

    The peace declaration in Shenzhen mentioned the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

    Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

    It has been revealed that another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi mentioned the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

    Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

    Elon Musk says SpaceX has a strategy to eliminate cell phone dead zones

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.
    • These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.
    • Recent findings suggest that “We’ve got a blueprint that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk remarked, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

    These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

    Recent findings suggest that “We’ve got a blueprint that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk remarked, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”.

    The organization’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

    Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he stated. According to Musk, the manufacturer has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”.

    Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”.

    The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

    SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell remarked during the tech giant’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use massive cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

    In a recent development, even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk mentioned one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

    SpaceX’s blueprint to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely newly introduced class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

    “I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he mentioned, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • South Korea's education ministry claims 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.
    • Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities stated on Friday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam.

    South Korea's education ministry claims 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.

    Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities stated on Friday.

    Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.

    Prior to the Suneung, authorities unveiled anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.

    On Friday, President Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.

    In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".

    Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

    Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.

    The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.

    These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

    His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

    "I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," remarked the candidate, 34-year-old Han Won-seok, in a video published on Sunday.

    His confession, days ahead of the Suneung, prompted authorities to introduce last-minute measures to prevent cheating during the national exam.

    The measures included nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

    Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

    The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

    It was the first time that South Korea tapped on its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

    Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

    All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

    Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times that he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

    Another told news outlet Yonhap that he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

    Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.

    Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.

    The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.

    Many South Koreans see the Suneung as a culmination of years of formal education - and a turning point that determines their university placements, careers, and social statuses.

    US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
    • Sources indicate that the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
    • According to recent reports, nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

    Sources indicate that the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

    According to recent reports, nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy intends to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

    Problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

    That caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

    An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a new router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

    It has been revealed that specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a new Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

    Industry observers note that FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union said that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

    Recent findings suggest that similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

    To get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

    (This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

    Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

    Industry observers note that philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

    It has been revealed that as an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

    It has been revealed that to kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

    And then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

    So you plan around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

    Sources indicate that and even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

    That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

    According to recent reports, it even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

    And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

    L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a big network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

    (Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

    I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

    So there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

    Now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

    Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

    It has been revealed that mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and states, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification? Does that mean they’ve been here for a certain period of time?” But they’ll figure that out, and the answer is not always the same.

    According to recent reports, so, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

    Maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a fresh hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

    Sources indicate that but this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

    It has been revealed that it’s crucial to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

    Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

    Sources indicate that mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has said that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

    According to recent reports, ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

    Mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

    But they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

    But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

    In a recent development, it is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

    Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

    I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

    Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

    Industry observers note that mann: An key caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

    Recent findings suggest that but what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not said it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

    One of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

    Sources indicate that so in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

    Do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that says a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

    According to recent reports, that’s the first major thing, and that should have taken whatever amount of time it took. Because the benefit with this kind of a system is that same basic impact assessment, you know, plus or minus maybe a couple of relatively small variables, is going to apply to every single one of these installations across the entire country. If they’re doing one of them or doing 1,000 of them, they’re all network-interconnected devices that all do the same thing and all hit the same network.

    So it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the new router significantly change anything? But it’s pretty easy from there.

    Sources indicate that then, and this is the notable part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

    So do it at midnight when, if you have a complete mass outage like this, it’s not too many travelers. Maybe a couple red-eye flights, a few cargo planes like UPS, FedEx, because those guys fly at night a lot, but it’s not 12,000 passenger planes.

    Industry observers note that that may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. If you’ve already done that kind of risk assessment, and you’ve briefed everybody accordingly, your technicians are sitting there in the building—hopefully they’re the right people—and they’re already braced to recover.

    Every time I started an engine generator that was going to run a radar site, I would hold my breath for a second when I flipped a switch, because things can happen. You can do everything right, and you flip a switch, and the engine throws a rod or something. Nothing you could do about it. Nothing you would know to prevent or anything like that. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

    Sources indicate that it is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

    You’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

    It has been revealed that in this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

    Ars Technica: The router installation matter that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

    Mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there. It’s kind of the paradox of risk analysis, right? The better you are at it, the less essential people think it is, and that’s the FAA being a victim of its own success for the last 50 years. I’m not in that camp that everything that sounds old needs to be replaced. Floppy disks are totally fine as long as they still work, I don’t care.

    But the agency has had a hard time modernizing, in part, I believe, because it is so safe and its risk management is normally so good that people lose sight of the fact that there isn’t modernization that needs to be done.

    In a recent development, it’s not that they don’t want to modernize, and it’s not like the FAA doesn’t want to modernize. It’s just that it’s the old squeaky wheel thing, right? The FAA is so good at what it does that when it comes time to write checks, there’s always a different squeaky wheel that needs the money more.

    Industry observers note that actually, I’m kind of happy for the current administration keeping this at the front. I don’t necessarily like how they’re doing it, but I do like that they’re making this a live issue in Congress. They’re making this a live issue even out here in different airports. I’ll talk to people and they’re like, “Hey, when are we going to modernize this?” Ten years ago, not too many people out in the public were talking about it.

    I think the NAS is still just as safe as it’s always been. We can kind of be grateful. Folks probably ought to understand that because they see this on the news, it means it’s weird. It’s unusual. But it’s good that we can be safe and we can still have the conversation about it, about what needs to happen to keep it safe, because we don’t want to have a catastrophic failure somewhere down the line that really is because something failed or really is because something was neglected, and then try to say, “Oh yeah, now we’ve got to shut down our airspace for six months because something happened.”.

    It has been revealed that I’m not a blank check person. I do not want [Congress] just writing a check and handing it to Duffy or anybody. I want them to do the proper acquisition oversight, do the proper union involvement, do the proper technical evaluations, all that kind of stuff, because that is money well spent.

    Sources indicate that we could have been really unlucky. We could have lost communication to all the aircraft that were in the air entirely. We could have lost the ability to be able to manage those aircraft, and then we would have been back to doing 1950s, 1960s kind of stuff, like call the airplane and have the airplane tell us where it is. And we probably would have seen some bad outcomes from that.

    Ars Technica: It is definitely sobering to think that this was in some ways the best-case scenario from the situation that unfolded.

    Mann: This was a best and worst [case]. In the resilience of the system, this was a best case because the system degraded all the way down to its essential mission of just keeping the aircraft safe. And an aircraft parked on the ground is as safe as it’s ever going to be, and the system was successful. The system is very resilient. It decayed down to its essential mission, and preserved that essential mission at the expense of literally everything else.

    The apparent lack of risk analysis is a very clear example of the worst case scenario. The network-spanning maintenance being done in the middle of the day and allowed to cascade as a failure into the entire NAS, that was horrible. So a single set of technologies failed, but the NAS itself showed its resilience in preserving that key mission all the way down to the minimum function, to the absolute zero, where the only piece left was just keep it safe. That’s what it’s supposed to do.

    Sources indicate that we don’t want to see it go that far down. We’d much rather have them just divert flights a couple minutes here and there. But if we need to get it all the way down to the only thing we have is safe aircraft, I’m good with that.

    It has been revealed that ars Technica: Duffy is saying the FAA needs $50 billion to make sure this doesn’t happen again. And if I understood correctly, you were saying it is good to have support for enough funding for the FAA to do what it needs to do, even if Duffy tying it specifically to “this happened because we didn’t have enough money” is not necessarily the correct assessment.

    In a recent development, mann: Yeah. This happened because there wasn’t the right oversight. I’d be pretty confident to say that. If we just take $50 billion and throw it at the same people doing the same thing the same way, we don’t get a better system. We just get a whole bunch more of this.

    Recent findings suggest that because hiring more contractors and getting more routers replaced faster in the middle of the day with no risk assessment and incorrect configurations or however it came about… take some of that money and put it into oversight, put it into testing, and put it into whatever you need to do to make sure that however many more of these we’re going to do are done properly, and in this case, at 2 o’clock in the morning with a team of qualified people with the proper testing, people ready to pull a plug on it, all that kind of stuff. That’s money well spent.

    Ars Technica: Many people have noted the coincidence of the FAA’s SMART AI system being deployed nationwide in the same week as the router glitch that led to the ground stop. The FAA has said the SMART rollout had no connection to what ensued. What is your view on all this?

    Mann: I get that. I think it is a coincidence. This particular router was just one of a long series of these replacements being done—they don’t take 1,000 routers and just replace them all on a Thursday. They might do one or two of them a night for a couple of years.

    Now, just to lean into it a little bit, it could be totally possible that the router’s capabilities, or maybe something that was configured or misconfigured, is a facilitating technology for SMART. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

    If you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

    It has been revealed that but you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

    According to recent reports, but the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

    Recent findings suggest that to the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

    Recent findings suggest that SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

    That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and states, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

    Industry observers note that this story was updated on November 20, 2026 to correct the description of the FAA ground stop’s impact on aircraft arrivals and departures. It was also updated to clarify one of Mann’s comments on the “move fast, break things” approach.

    #12539. Tech Report: Anthropic rival claims companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
